articles.summary: I usually give a talk by reading it, with the slides behind me. For a short slot tonight I would like to try something else: a talk that is completely scripted, where the slides, the builds, the animations and even the demo play on a clock, and I speak to them instead of reading from them. This grows out of two talks already published as vaults on sgit.ai. The Black Hat Europe 2025 keynote made the slides data: 26 slides in one JSON file that the app reads at load time, with ten versions of the slide system beside it. The VoiceDebrief pitch added a presenter with per-slide timings, a countdown and speaker notes, built from a template by a script. The next step is to make the whole talk a timeline. This site's agent built a first version: one HTML file that plays a file of beats, each with a start, a duration, a slide and the words to say, with builds, a terminal that types a command and prints its recorded output, tables that reveal row by row, video, and a presenter view with the words, the seconds left and what comes next. A rehearsal mode records planned against actual times. The first timeline is the five-minute demo for ruv.sgit.ai, the newest site in the sgit family, built for tonight's Agentic Engineering Live with rUv in London. And Claude Motion, which Anthropic released in beta on 8 October, makes the animations the same way: as code, exported as MP4.

articles.title: The tokens hook: a token behaviour policy that shows what every session reads, caches, writes and costs, why a prompt cannot do it, and a brief for tokens.hook.sgit.ai
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A token behaviour policy as a 132-line hook: the user sees what each session reads, caches and costs; a prompt cannot do it.
articles.summary: It is easy to spend a lot of money on model calls without seeing where it goes, and the user is the person who sees least. So I asked for a small, focused agent behaviour policy about tokens: in observe mode first, it should show the user, in a box of ASCII under each answer, how many tokens the session has read, how many came from the cache, how many it wrote, how big the context is and roughly what it has cost. This site's agent built it as a Claude Code hook of 132 lines with a policy file, and tested it. A prompt cannot do this job: asked to report its own usage, the model said twice, correctly, that it could not see the numbers. The hook gave it the exact figures, one turn behind, in about a millisecond. Building it found a bug in our own session report, which had been counting every response two or three times, because the transcript repeats a response's usage on each of its content blocks. It also found that, in this version of Claude Code, the transcript a hook can read carries the system prompt and every tool definition, though the documentation does not say so. This session has read 99% of its input from the cache, which at list prices is the difference between about $170 and about $1,950. The other tools vary: Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor have hooks and usage commands, the chat apps show only limits. And this is the brief for tokens.hook.sgit.ai, a small site for a small, mission-critical piece of code.

articles.title: Cedar and the policy vault: a debrief on the policy language agents are adopting, where our behaviour policies and sgit vaults meet it, and a brief for the MVP
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Cedar is mature and adopted; it lacks the why, the version in force and the evidence. A vault carries all three, and the demo shows it working.
articles.summary: Cedar is the policy language I think we should adopt rather than compete with. AWS open-sourced it in May 2023 under Apache 2.0; it joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a Sandbox project on 8 October 2025; it is the language of Amazon Verified Permissions and of AgentCore Policy, which checks every agent tool call before it runs; and its design is modelled and proved in Lean. That is a mature environment, and it already says most of what our agent behaviour policies say: permit for the grant, forbid for the barrier, a schema for the footprint. What it does not carry is why a rule exists, which version was in force, or the evidence of what it decided. Those are exactly what an encrypted, versioned vault is good at. So I asked this site's agent to try it: Cedar policies, schema, entities and tests in an sgit vault, a gate that refuses any version that fails validation, tags signed by the releasing clone, enforcement points that clone with a read key and cannot write, and an append lane that keeps a sealed, hash-chained record of every decision. It worked on a local server, and it found one thing worth knowing: Cedar skips a policy whose evaluation fails, so a forbid that refers to a missing attribute lets the action through. This article is the debrief, the crosswalk between their terms and ours, and the brief for the agent that will build the MVP.

articles.title: The citizen developer is good news: the spreadsheet grown up, the best briefs ever written, and the handover from explorers to villagers and town planners that makes them last
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The citizen developer is the spreadsheet grown up: the best briefs ever written, handed to villagers and town planners, carried in versioned vaults.
articles.summary: At a conference today the phrase "citizen developer" came up as a worry, the new name for people outside IT building things they should not. I think it is one of the best things to happen to software, and a better way to talk about what is usually called vibe coding. It is not only citizens: it is the employee, the business owner, the expert, the person who knows the work. People have always built with what they controlled, and for most of them that was a spreadsheet; spreadsheets are full of errors, and the world runs on them anyway, because they were the only tool people had. Now they can build full applications, and those applications are also the best briefs ever written: what the user actually wants, in a form that runs. The work is the handover, from the explorer who built it to the villagers who harden it and the town planners who make it scale, with all the non-functional requirements the explorer never had to think about. Encrypted, versioned vaults are a natural carrier for that: a mini app with its UI and its data in one place, which is what a spreadsheet always was, with history, keys and a clean handover added. Done well, this lets people, organisations and even countries move from rent-seeking, control-based software to tools that serve them, which is also the direction of the business models this newsroom is testing.

articles.title: Paying after the value: why a balance that can go negative feels different from a subscription, the psychology behind it, and the experiment this newsroom is running
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Most purchases are bets on future value; a reading balance that can go negative asks for payment when the value is already in view.
articles.summary: Almost every time I buy something, I am buying future value. A subscription, a gym membership, a big security product on a good deal, even a one-off purchase: I am betting that I will use it enough for the price of each use to fall to a number I am comfortable with. Often I lose the bet, and the cost of unsubscribing keeps me paying. The research agrees: gym members on a monthly contract paid more than $17 a visit when they could have paid $10. This newsroom is trying the opposite. You start with £5 of credit, each article you read uses a few pence, you can set the price from free to double or refuse it, and the balance can go below zero and stay there. By the time you are asked to pay, you have the value in front of you: what you read, how much, what you liked. The payment is connected to what you received, not what you hope to receive. That only works where the cost of serving is close to zero, which is true of a static site on a CDN, and where the value adds up in a way the reader can see. Wikipedia is the counter-example: £20 a year asked for at a moment with no value in view, even though it is a few pence an article. Add prices fair by country, the Big Mac index for reading, and a view of where the money goes, and payment becomes a choice people are glad to make. The experiment is live, with written hypotheses and a review in December, and I will report back.

articles.title: The eyeballs get cheap: why open source is about to become the most secure software we have, and why secure, sovereign and paid-for meet at the least code in production
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Cheap, deep AI security review gives open source the eyeballs it never had; with sovereignty and paid maintenance, all point at the least code in production.
articles.summary: For as long as I have worked in security there has been no clear winner between open source and proprietary software. Open source had the code in view, and fixes that sweep a bug's variants; it also had very few people and almost no budget for the slow, expensive reviews that find the hard bugs. Proprietary software had the budget, and the cover of being hidden, and got away with a lot. That balance just moved. Models can now run deep security reviews over and over, on every project, at a cost that used to buy one consultant for a day. The thing open source lacked was paid attention, and that is the thing that just became abundant. I thought Chainguard had started publishing the projects where its AI found nothing; I could not find that. What I found is better: the maintainer of curl writing about a year in which AI review first drowned his project in noise, then produced hundreds of real fixes, then a frontier scan that found a single low-severity bug, and then, today, deeper tools finding more. That is what a project getting harder to break looks like. Put it next to two things I have argued before, that sovereignty needs open code and open schemas, and that the business is maintaining the version each customer actually runs, and three forces meet at one place: the least amount of code in production.

articles.title: Commander's intent is a behaviour policy: Sondera's argument in our words, the business layer above it, and five of our rules compiled to Cedar and tested
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Sondera's commander's intent and our behaviour policies are one idea: twelve terms joined, the business layer above, and five rules tested in Cedar.
articles.summary: Josh Devon of Sondera published an article today that states clearly the problem we keep writing about. Agents do not go rogue; they follow the instructions they were given and fill the gaps with whatever gets the job done. The military solved this a long time ago with commander's intent, the objective and its limits written down together, and agents inherited the initiative and none of the limits. His answer is to write the limits about effects, not actions, compile them into rules a machine can check, and enforce them outside the agent before every action. We are talking about the same thing in different words, so I joined the two vocabularies: twelve of their terms against ours, most of them the same idea, and two places where one side goes further. We go further up, into the business layer, where an agent's limits stop being universal and become how a company does invoices and who it is in dispute with. They go further in proof, compiling plain English into Cedar and checking it with a theorem prover. To show the two halves meeting, I wrote five rules as Cedar, their published example, two from this session's own policy, one from the skill policy I published today and two from our business layer, and evaluated fourteen requests against them. All fourteen came out as intended. The incidents behind their argument check out against Anthropic's and the UK AI Security Institute's own reports, with a few figures rounded differently.

articles.title: A skill behaviour policy: what a skill says it does, what it can do, what it is given, and the control that closes the gap, measured on 899 skills
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A skill behaviour policy compares what a skill says, what it can do and what it is given, then generates the control; measured on 899 skills.
articles.summary: I saw a video today that said "1 in 20 Claude skills are built to hack your computer". It is an overstatement of a real study, and the real finding is interesting enough: in one large study of public marketplaces, 5.2% of the skills analysed showed "high-severity patterns strongly suggesting malicious intent". It made me think about what an agent behaviour policy can do for skills. A skill behaviour policy looks at three things. The mandate the description promises; the mandate the skill actually has, from what its instructions and files can do, treated as features; and the grant, which depends on where it runs. The gap between the first two is the suspicious part; the gap between the last two is the reach nobody asked for. Then the policy becomes a control: a hook and a sandbox setting, generated from the described mandate, that bring the grant down to what you expected. I built a static calculator and ran it on 899 public skills from three sources: 812 can reach something beyond their own scripts, 782 of them through one third-party tool server, and 39 have a feature their description does not mention. None was obfuscated. The clearest case was honest: a skill that reads your Claude Code chat history, searches HackerNews and sends a report to Slack has the whole lethal trifecta, says so, and still needs a control. NVIDIA's scanner rated it safe, which is right for the question a scanner asks. A policy asks a different one.

articles.title: sgit in GitHub Actions, side by side: a showcase repository and site that runs four ways of moving a vault between jobs on every run, measured, with a budget for its LLM steps
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A showcase repository that runs four ways of moving a vault between GitHub Actions jobs side by side, measured, with a budget for its LLM steps.
articles.summary: sgit in a CI pipeline described how an encrypted vault can carry data in and out of GitHub Actions, and between its jobs. The next step is to show it running, and to keep showing it. So this is a brief for a dedicated repository and website, just for that: its own issues, its own CI pipeline, and on every run four ways of moving a vault between jobs, side by side, in parallel. A vault server with the keys in the repository's secrets; the encrypted vault itself as an artefact, a zip that one job uploads and the next downloads; the vault published as files and cloned read-only from any web host; and append lanes for jobs that only need to hand results in. Each lane reports its time, its bytes, the keys each job held and a screenshot, and repeats on vaults of growing size with full, thin and path clones. I measured the core of it locally for this article. A clone of one folder barely grows with the vault: 0.59 seconds at 100 files, 0.77 at 2,000. A full clone grows with it, from 0.95 to 5.55 seconds. The repository should also have a budget, because some steps will call models, from more than one provider, and every token they spend should be counted against it.

articles.title: Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults: seven architectures from one agent to a swarm, a repository of recipes that gates sgit's releases, and what a hundred writers did to an append lane
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Seven architectures for agents on ephemeral vaults, a recipe repository that gates sgit's releases, and a hundred writers measured on an append lane.
articles.summary: There is a pattern I keep using for agents that work together: give them an encrypted vault as their shared memory and their way of talking, and let it exist only for as long as the work does. I would like to capture it properly, as a series of architectures from simple to complex, each in a repository of its own with its agents, its keys, its fixtures and a CI job that proves it works, so that people and agents can fork them as templates, recipes and skills. The repository should run as one of the checks before anything reaches sgit's main branch. The key questions are the same at every level: how do you give agents shared memory, how do they communicate, how do they work asynchronously, and how do you know what each one is doing at any moment. The answer depends on who holds which key. Because the only thing that ever leaves the environment is ciphertext, you can be more relaxed about where the logs and the data go: it is all about the keys, and about whether the vault is ephemeral. A vault app can draw what the agents are doing, and the screenshot can go back into the vault. And I wanted to know how far it scales, so we measured it locally: a hundred writers posting ten entries each landed a thousand entries in an append lane in 4.9 seconds, none lost. The same test found four defects, which is the case for the release gate in one paragraph.

articles.title: Hooks are kernel code: a maturity model, the first ten hooks mapped, and a brief for a hooks site and feed where you pay for state, never to run
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Hooks are small code with kernel reach: a maturity model, the first ten hooks mapped, and a brief for a hooks site where you pay for state, never to run.
articles.summary: The hooks we are now going to deploy are code, and very critical code. They are also a very good example of code that is simple in many ways: a hook can be five lines. That makes them a good case study for everything we do on code review, code practices, semantic graphs and change blast radius, because the problem is small enough to do completely. A hook runs on every matching action, with the user's permissions, and can see, block or rewrite what the agent does; we should treat it like kernel code. Hooks also range from completely deterministic scripts to hooks that call a model or a whole agent, so I propose a maturity model: five levels from the prompt to off the machine, and three questions for every hook, how much power it has, which legs of the lethal trifecta it touches, and how much sandbox it runs in. I mapped the first ten: three this session runs, five tested in a sandbox, two proposed. They are between 4 and 26 lines, and the smallest of them depend on much more: the eleven-line commit hook calls a 37-line scan, so one line changed in the scan moves the commit gate for every session. And this is a brief for a site and a feed to manage them, like a skills manager: every hook from its intent, with its graph, tests, version and signature, installable anywhere, and a billing model where nobody pays to run a hook, but paying buys state.

articles.title: Chainguard, mapped: what it builds, what it publishes, how far up the stack its context goes, and where an open behaviour policy and an encrypted vault could plug in
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Chainguard mapped from OS to agents, its public feeds counted, and the context layer above the package where an open policy and a vault fit.
articles.summary: Chainguard is one of the companies doing the most interesting work in software supply chain security, and much of it is open: the Wolfi distribution, public advisory feeds, Sigstore in its lineage, and a growing set of products for agents. So I mapped it: the company, what it builds from the operating system up to agents, what data it publishes that anyone can read, and how deep that data goes. I read the feeds and counted them. 12,480 advisories covering 12,125 distinct CVEs; in a sample, about seven in ten findings marked fixed and one in five marked as not applying. And in the archived Wolfi advisories, where the reasons were public, 2,850 determinations that a vulnerability did not apply, of which 177 gave a reason about context: the vulnerable code is not in the execution path, an attacker cannot control it, or it is mitigated. That is where the graph stops, and it is the question that matters to me. As with everything in security, it is about context. An image with many vulnerabilities is fine if the application on top never reaches them; one reachable flaw is not. Deciding which images are non-negotiable and which can ship today needs a graph from the user story, through the code and its dependencies, to the container. That context layer is where an open behaviour policy and an encrypted vault fit, next to the agent products Chainguard is now shipping, which already talk about policies. I make the case for each.

articles.title: The wire as a graph: start from what the reader sees, give every story and every name a long-lived ID, link every phrase of a short narrative, and a brief for the desks
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Design the wire from what the reader sees: every name a link with a long-lived ID, every sentence a claim, stories of stories, folders by gravity.
articles.summary: The wires already collect the day's news into encrypted vaults on a schedule. This is the next step, and the way to design it is to start at the end, with what the reader sees, and work backwards to the data. A story should read as a short narrative in which every name is a link, to a person, a company, an event or a place, each with a long-lived ID, and every sentence is a claim with its evidence: a fact, an observation, a statement by a party, or our analysis. Stories group into stories, and that is the fractal part: a thread is a story made of stories, and an article someone else published is a story too. From there, the primitives: a run that collects, captures that freeze what was read, claims, stories, stories of stories and names, each with a random ID that never changes. I measured the four wires' public vaults today: 202 stories, 1,358 distinct names, only 171 of them in more than one story and 48 in more than one wire, and only 44% of the names a story lists appear in its own text. Those numbers say where the work is, and how big a folder tree it needs: a name gets its own folder when it has gravity. Earlier experiments that linked every word of a long text were the right idea done too much. A wire story's narrative is about 55 words, small enough to link every phrase. Cheaper models can do the heavy lifting and a more capable one can check it. This article is also the brief for the desks and the wire agent.

articles.title: System prompts as behaviour policies: Claude's published prompt and a leaked ChatGPT one, mapped into rows, a taxonomy of rules, and a JSON file a harness could enforce
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Claude's published system prompt as 82 policy rows in eight kinds: 36 could be held by the harness, 21 partly by classifiers, 25 stay with the model.
articles.summary: I have said before that a system prompt is a light behaviour policy. So I tested it. The hypothesis: can an existing system prompt be represented as an agent behaviour policy, and if so, what should that look like as a JSON file that models can read and harnesses can enforce, with stronger controls in more places than the prompt itself? Anthropic publishes Claude's system prompts, so the test used the real one: Claude Haiku 5.5's, published on 7 October 2026. It holds 4,255 words and 82 rules. Sorted by kind, 36 of them, about tool use, conversation state, referrals, knowledge and input trust, could be held by the harness rather than by the model's good behaviour; 21 harm restrictions could be held in part by classifiers outside the model, which Anthropic already uses; and 25, about judgement and presentation, stay with the model. For contrast, a leaked ChatGPT prompt, unverified, is the opposite shape: about six words in seven sit under its tool sections. Between them they are the two halves of a behaviour policy, the rules and the reach. What neither has is a mandate, a statement of who may override whom that the harness can check, or a record of what keeps each rule. So I propose an ontology and a taxonomy for it, and a JSON shape. And I looked for anyone running a written agent behaviour policy for real: the formats are arriving, the published policies are not.

articles.title: The agents write too: lessons, debriefs and a page for every agent on the newsroom, and a brief for the conductor that will keep it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The newsroom's agents get their own bylines: lessons every agent loads, debriefs as source material, a page for every agent, and a conductor.
articles.summary: The newsroom is no longer one agent. I split the work into focused sessions, a writer, a wire, a designer, a newsletter, each told "you are now this agent, and you only do this", and git merges what they do, with the occasional small conflict. That works well, and it has created two problems. The agents now learn things the others should know, and each of them does so much that I need a debrief. So the newsroom gets a new area and a new workflow. There will be two kinds of article: the ones under my name, written from my voice memos and reviewed by me, and the ones an agent writes under its own name about what it did, linked to its own page. Agents write lessons, one lesson each, which every agent reads at the start of its next session: memory, in its plainest form. They write debriefs, which are also the source material for my articles. Their articles can carry what other agents need, briefs, references, graphs, IDs and JSON. A page keeps track of every agent. And a new agent, the conductor, keeps the site and writes every time it runs. Whether the agents should run every day is a decision for later, once the debriefs show what a run is worth. This article is also the brief for the session that builds it.

articles.title: Are hooks the sweet spot? Moving an agent's rules from hope into hooks, rule by rule, until enforcement moves off the machine
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: One agent's eleven rules, moved from the prompt into hooks and tested: four fully, two mostly, three partly, two not at all, and a gap in the leak scan.
articles.summary: Most of the rules we give agents today are hope-based security: written in the prompt, kept only if the model keeps them. The agent writing this site works under a behaviour policy of eleven rules, and only one of them is kept by something other than the agent. So I asked the question directly: in October 2026, are hooks the sweet spot? Can we move the rules out of the prompt and into small deterministic programs the agent's harness runs before and after every action, and keep them there until enforcement moves into a gateway or the platform itself? I took this session's own policy and tried, rule by rule, in a throwaway repository. Four rules moved into hooks fully, two mostly, three partly and two not at all, and the tests found a gap in the check I trust most. Hooks are the first layer that does not rely on the model and the last that still sees the action in the agent's own terms, which is why I think they are the right place to start, provided they are installed where the agent cannot edit them and set to fail closed. The open hook collections that exist block dangerous commands; the step that is missing is generating hooks from a written policy, and testing them, so the same rules can later be enforced by a gateway. We already need this for our own agents, so we can be among its heaviest users.

articles.title: Agent hooks in October 2026: a technical debrief on what each platform lets you see, stop and change, where hooks run, and where they fail
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A debrief on agent hooks across ten platforms: what each can see, stop and change, where they run, and the failure modes every vendor admits.
articles.summary: More and more of the technical people I talk to who are trying to control agents for real are reaching for the same tool: hooks, small programs the agent's harness runs at fixed points, before a tool call, after it, when a prompt is submitted, when the agent stops. This is the debrief I wanted to read: the lay of the land on 14 October 2026, from each vendor's own documentation. The short version is that the design has converged. Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf), Grok Build, Factory, Augment and Kiro all offer a hook before a tool call that can block it, and most can ask the user or rewrite the call. They differ where it matters for security: whether an organisation can force its own hooks and switch everyone else's off, whether a failing hook blocks or lets the action through, whether hooks shipped in a repository need trust before they run, and whether anything can see the model's own output. ChatGPT offers admin controls rather than hooks, and Lovable gates publishing rather than agent actions. The vendors and the people who publish hook collections say the same thing about their limits: guardrails, not walls. Hooks see what the harness routes through them, run with the user's permissions, fail open by default on most tools, and have been an attack surface themselves. I ran a small test of my own in a throwaway repository, and the companion article asks what this means for agent behaviour policies.

articles.title: Knowledge that maintains itself: semantic graphs for an organisation's policies and internal knowledge, briefing people and agents from the graph, and vaults to carry the brief
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Fractal semantic graphs for policies and internal knowledge: brief people and agents from the graph, maintain it in a loop, carry the brief in a vault.
articles.summary: In a conversation today I tried to put in a few sentences what all the graph work on this site is for, and it came out as knowledge management. Take an organisation's policies and internal information, and build a fractal semantic graph of it: an ontology and a taxonomy for every element, each part kept in its own vocabulary, with named edges between them. Then brief people and agents from the graph, not from the pile of documents. They get the slice they need and the diff since they last read it, so the context is there and the tokens are not wasted. It looks a bit like vector search, but vectors give you similarity, not a reason, and the answer can change with the model and the index; a graph gives the same answer to the same question and the path that led to it. The most important part is that the feedback loop maintains itself. You do not have to get the graph right first; you have to maintain it, and agents are very good at maintaining graphs. When something in the graph looks wrong, you ask why, and the answer is a fix at the right altitude. I measured the briefing on this site: the graphs of its 112 articles hold about an eighth of the articles' text. And the brief has to travel. That is what sgit is for: an encrypted git where I give an agent the key to a vault, it reads and writes there, I can scope it to one folder and encrypt to it with its own key, and the vault itself says, this is what you need to read now.

articles.title: The minimum code below: container security from the top down, from the user story to the immutable line, measured on one real tool
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Container security from the top down: at every layer, keep only the code the layer above needs. Measured on one real tool, with its limits.
articles.summary: A conversation at Chainguard's event today sharpened something I have thought for a while. Chainguard does security from the bottom up, and does it very well: it rebuilds the operating system and the libraries from source, keeps the images minimal and manages the whole process. But even the most locked-down image still holds a great deal of code the application never runs, the assurance still depends on testing, and the loop that caused the problem in the first place is still there: when something breaks, you give it more. As soon as the work reaches the application, it stops. My proposal is to come from the other end. Start from the user story and, at every layer down, ask one question: what is the minimum code below this that the layer above needs? Keep that, remove everything else, and draw the immutable line as high as the evidence allows. It did not scale before; with models and fractal semantic graphs, it can. I measured it for this article on a real tool, sgit and its dependencies, running a CI-style use case under coverage and then running it again from a tree holding only the files that ran. Of 1,500 files, 428 were kept, and the use case passed; commands outside it failed because their code was not there. It also showed the limits: one compiled binary held three quarters of the bytes and no coverage tool can see inside it, and coverage missed a compiled module the tests then caught. Tools that minimise containers at run time already exist, so the new part is the direction: from what the application is for, through a graph, down to a build that can be certified. Chainguard is unusually well placed to offer it, and someone will build it.

articles.title: A policy for every skill: Sean Turner's natural-language control for agent skills, the behaviour policy behind it, and using models to need them less
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Sean Turner's natural-language control for agent skills, read as a behaviour policy, and why the description, not the code, stays canonical.
articles.summary: I was with my friend Sean Turner this week, talking about agent behaviour policies, and he described something he built that I think is great. It is a natural-language control policy for agent skills, and a CI pipeline that checks every skill contributed to an organisation-wide repository against it before hundreds of developers pull it down to their machines. Is it safe, secure, well documented, usable, understandable by the model and understandable by people. And the part that makes it more than a linter: it reads the skill in its context. A skill that turns internal documentation into a LinkedIn post has no untrusted input to worry about; a skill that pulls content off the web is handling untrusted text, and should treat it as data, not obey it. It sits beside a security scan, not instead of one: the question is operational, is this the right way to give this skill to our workforce. That is an agent behaviour policy for a skill: the mandate is what the skill is for, the reach is everything it touches, and the gap is the risk. A control written in natural language is hope-based security, better than nothing and not enough on its own. Sean's next step is the one I keep coming back to: use an agent to write deterministic rules that follow the natural-language control, and keep the description, not the code, as the canonical version. Change the description, regenerate the code. Using models to need them less. And in a common ontology, a whole catalogue of skills becomes one graph, where the dangerous combinations are a query.

articles.title: Policy as code needs a policy first: what an agent behaviour policy adds, and how to reverse engineer one from the code, the spreadsheet or the paper you already have
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Policy as code answers one question. An agent behaviour policy holds the rest, and can be generated into code or reverse engineered from it.
articles.summary: At an event this week a speaker described policy as code as the way to scale governance and AI innovation together, and it clicked. Policy as code is right, and it is where agent governance has to end up. But for agents it answers one question, is this request allowed, and the questions a business, an auditor or an insurer asks are the ones around it, the ones an Agent Behaviour Policy holds. What can this agent reach, measured. What was it asked to do, and why. Where the two differ. Which rules can no engine ever see. And the one that surprised me when I checked: for every rule that is code, who can change that code. A rule the agent can rewrite is a setting, not a control. Because an ABP has those columns, it can be written in both directions. From the policy, generate code: for this article, five rows of a real ABP became a Rego policy that Open Policy Agent ran against seven requests, denying a push to the wrong repository, a commit without a leak scan and a model id in a diff, asking before a pull request, and allowing a sentence no engine can judge. From what exists, reverse engineer the policy: parse the code back, and the gaps show on both sides, a row with no code and a rule nobody wrote a reason for. I did it to this session's own policy: of its eleven rules, eight have some code behind them, and only one has code the agent cannot change. Fractal semantic graphs are what make the round trip work across paper, spreadsheets, regulations and code, because each keeps its own vocabulary and the edges between them carry verbs both ways.

articles.title: sgit in a CI pipeline: encrypted, versioned data in and out of GitHub Actions, between its jobs, through write-only lanes, and a key for every job
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Encrypted, versioned vaults as the way data gets into, out of and between CI jobs, with a key per job and a sidecar when there is no server.
articles.summary: Getting data in and out of a CI pipeline is harder than it should be. GitHub Actions has artifacts, kept 90 days by default and deleted with their run; caches, 10 GB per repository and evicted after a week unused; and job outputs, at most 1 MB per job. Each is fine for its job, and none is a versioned, encrypted record that a person, an auditor or another pipeline can read from outside GitHub. This article maps how sgit vaults fill that gap, and every pattern in it was run for the article against a local vault server. A job pushes what it produced to a vault, and anything with the read key can clone it from anywhere, with history. Jobs pass data to each other through the same vault, each cloning only the folders it needs with --path, which is a large saving in time and in what lands on the runner, though it is a speed setting rather than a boundary. The boundaries are the keys: a read key clones and cannot commit; an append token, one per test shard, adds to its own write-only inbox and reads nothing; and each job can have its own key pair, so a deploy configuration encrypted to the deploy job fails to decrypt anywhere else, and a signed manifest fails verification once it is changed. Even done a little loosely, that turns wiring mistakes into loud failures. The keys come from secrets on stdin, and only the ciphertext half of a vault ever leaves the runner. And when you would rather not depend on a hosted server, the vault server runs as a sidecar whose storage folder holds only ciphertext: archive it into the Actions cache, an artifact or a git branch, and the next run restores it with its full history.

articles.title: The homepage is a vault: a fresh edition every morning, every past homepage one commit away, served from plain files, and a brief for the agent that builds it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A new homepage edition every morning, each a signed commit in a vault, served from plain files: every past homepage one commit id away.
articles.summary: The homepage of this site has to be fresh every day, and today it changes only when someone releases the site. I would like a job that runs every morning at about 05:45, reads the latest articles, the wires and what is happening in the industry, and writes a new edition of the homepage. And that homepage should be a vault. Every edition a commit with a signed tag and its own version line; every edition carrying the links it showed and why, a screenshot of itself and the release note that explains it; any past homepage one commit id away; variants side by side for A/B tests; and anyone who wants their own homepage, in another language or for another audience, forks the vault. The encrypted objects can be served as plain files from S3, a CDN or GitHub Pages, read in the browser with a published read key. I had two facts wrong: this site is not served by a Lambda, it is on GitHub Pages; the Lambda is the vault API the wire reads through, and that is where the time goes, at 317 milliseconds a request against 44 for a static file. This site's agent built the homepage vault locally: three editions, three signed tags, a static export, and a browser that rendered today's edition in four requests, yesterday's in three, and nothing at all inside two minutes. A stats lane took 300 page-load beacons. This is the design, the measurements, and the brief.

articles.title: Attacks rewritten as mandates: 28 supply-chain incidents, the column each one was missing, and why the next maintainer is an agent
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: 28 supply-chain attacks read as reach beyond mandate: what a hardened registry stops, what only a written mandate can, and why agents change it.
articles.summary: Chainguard keeps a public ledger of software supply-chain attacks, 28 incidents from May 2024 to October 2026, 23 of them this year. I read it the way I read an agent's permissions, and every row turns out to be the same shape. A credential, a tag or a build step could do far more than it was ever meant to do, and the attacker used the difference. A maintainer token that could publish any version of any package, used by someone whose job was to release one SDK from a reviewed build. That is reach beyond mandate, the gap an Agent Behaviour Policy is written to make visible. Sorted by what would have stopped each attack, by our reading, a control on the consumer's side, a hardened registry, a cooldown, no install scripts, appears in 26 of the 28; a control on the publisher's side, a written answer to what a credential was for, appears in 16. The first kind is a product you can buy. The second is a document almost nobody has written. And it matters more every month, because the next maintainer holding a publish token is an agent: Chainguard's own engineers describe a fleet that opened 4,746 pull requests in eight weeks against their code, fenced by rules that are an excellent mandate, kept in prompts, bot configuration and a blog post. One pipeline needs three records: trusted inputs, a written mandate, and provable outputs with a memory that outlives the session. As an open source project we would like to be on the first list, and this article is about the other two.

articles.title: Four frameworks, one agent: iason's comparison of the OECD classification, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act, read against what runs here, with the evidence and the graphs
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: iason's comparison of four AI risk frameworks, mapped to the behaviour policy, the footprint and the graphs that run here, with the status of each row.
articles.summary: A paper reached me this week, AI Risk Management Frameworks, issue 81 of iason's research series, dated November 2025, by Sara Martucci and Margherita Ranieri with Nicola Mazzoni. It reads four instruments side by side, the OECD's classification of AI systems, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, Japan's AI Guidelines for Business and the EU AI Act, and ends with five principles they share, ethics and human rights, the lifecycle, human oversight, risk tiering with proportionality, and governance as an organisational habit rather than a compliance exercise. I agree with the five, and the paper's own list of what most companies still lack, AI-specific KPIs, a formal adoption and risk strategy, a central governance function and a process for reviewing AI outputs, is the list I would write. So this article does what the frameworks ask of a deployer, on the one system I can show: a newsroom run by agents, and the agent team that runs my correspondence, both under a written behaviour policy. I take each framework's question and answer it with what runs here, the evidence behind it and the graphs we have already built, and I say where the answer is a design or an argument rather than a thing that runs. Two things come out of the mapping. The frameworks' unit is the AI system, classified before deployment; for an agent in a loop with tools the unit has to be one agent in one deployment, and its risk is its reach, measured, with a blast radius for each row. And the questions the frameworks leave open, who holds the residual risk, until when, and on what evidence, are the ones the behaviour policy, the footprint and the risk acceptance record were built to answer. The paper is also, in this site's own terms, a page that needs a status since: it was written before the Act's dates moved.

articles.title: Every link points back: 566 links between 105 articles, 15 that point forward, and why an article should know what came next and what corrected it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: 551 of 566 links between articles point back in time. Why older articles should say what came next and what corrected them.
articles.summary: I tend to write these articles in sequence, and I think of them as reading in sequence. Then I go back to one and realise there is no path from it to the next, because the earlier article cannot know what came after it. So we counted. Across the 105 articles on this site there are 566 links from one article to another, written into the text, and 551 of them point back in time. Only 15 point forward, and every one of those was added later, by an edit. 94 of the 105 articles are cited by a later one, 551 citations in all, and 11 of them are answered by a link the other way. Of 104 pairs of articles published one after the other, the later one links to the earlier one 42 times; the earlier one links to the later one 7 times. That is by design: a link is written when the article is written, and the future does not exist yet. The site already derives a Continued by list at the foot of every article, so the path exists, but it sits below the sources, it does not say why, and it treats a correction the same as a passing mention. Corrections matter most. We found three kinds: an article revised in place, which the version pages already show; a later article correcting an earlier one, of which there is one clear case and its earlier article does point to it; and the quieter one, a plan described in one article that a later article says has not happened. So this release adds What came next notes at the top of the four articles I wrote in a row today, and proposes four kinds of forward link, so that the graph of articles can be read in both directions.

articles.title: Sixteen notes I did not want to lose: a request to send from any browser to my vault, why identity is still this hard, and how two more wires became a product line
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Sixteen notes stuck in a browser with no passkey led to a request: let any browser send to my vault, by link, text or QR code.
articles.summary: I opened the newsroom on my iPhone, in a browser that looked like Chrome but could not reach my passkeys, and the vault button told me there were sixteen changes that existed only in that browser. My reaction is the most interesting part: those were notes and reads I wanted to keep. They had become pieces of intelligence, and I was happy to do a couple of steps to get them into my vault, as long as I only had to do it once. That is the nudge working for the right reason. So this is a feature request and a brief. Every reader vault should have a lane that any browser can write to, by a link, a piece of text or a QR code carrying only where to write and the key to encrypt with, so that a browser with no passkey, no sign-in, or an old operating system can send what it holds into my vault, and the vault takes it from there the next time I open it. The newsroom already does exactly this to send a reading summary to sgit.ai, so it is a pattern pointed at myself. It is also a commentary. Identity is still a mess: passkeys that work in one browser and not in the one an app opens a link in, and an email connector that makes attachments, inline images and a clean reply in a thread far harder than the underlying service does. Users will accept a lot of friction, once, when the value is clear, which is how WhatsApp links a computer and how Midjourney grew on a Discord bot. What they will not accept is losing their data. And the other half of the day's news is the opposite story: two new wires, OWASP and AWS, built from two small config files on the same pipeline, and suddenly a new product line.

articles.title: The human in the loop is a spectrum: how cheap it is to undo decides where a person belongs, and why the newsroom ships on its own while my email still waits for me
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: How much to let an agent ship on its own depends on how cheap it is to undo and how mature the controls are, and both of those move.
articles.summary: Writing about the human in the loop, we noticed something about our own workflow: this newsroom arrived, organically, at releasing on its own, fourteen times in one day, with nobody approving each release, while every email my agents write still waits for me to press send. I think that contrast goes to the heart of the question, and it is a spectrum, not a switch. A useful test for how much to let go is how cheap it is to undo. I remember a senior executive, I think from Google, whose test for people asking to start a project or an experiment was exactly that: if it does not reach many people and can be switched off with little side effect, say yes, trust the people, have a go, because the only cost is the time and there is always learning; what worried him was how hard it would be to undo. Amazon put the same idea as one-way and two-way doors. An email is a one-way door: once it goes, you cannot claim it back, a mistake does damage straight away, and my email workflow is still in the explorer phase, with nascent controls and not yet many emails read and sent without changes. The newsroom is a two-way door: a correction is a new version, anyone who arrives after the fix gets the fixed page, few people are reading yet, new articles land in the latest list without being placed on the front page, and the checks and balances are mature, from the validator to the leak scan to briefing packs that hand work between sites. When I read an article, I am either happy with it or I make small changes; I have not yet read one and thought I do not want that live. So the spectrum has two axes, the cost of undoing and the maturity of the controls and the record, and both move: as readership grows the newsroom's side effects grow with it, and as the email controls mature, email can move the other way.

articles.title: The human in the loop, safety net or bottleneck: both, until you decide which outputs need a person and give that person the why
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Checking every output is a bottleneck and a weak safety net; put the person where it cannot be undone, and let controls do the rest.
articles.summary: Someone shaping a roundtable in London asked me this week for my thoughts on a question that keeps coming up: is the human in the loop a safety net or a bottleneck? Plenty of companies have agent pilots that look great, and very few trust an agent to make a real decision without someone checking every output. My answer is that a person checking every output is both, and is mostly neither: it is a bottleneck because it does not scale, and it is a weak safety net because people approve almost everything they are shown, which Anthropic measured at 93% of permission prompts. The question is not whether there is a human in the loop. It is which outputs need one, what that person is given to decide with, and what moves the line over time. Put the person where an output cannot be undone and the blast radius is large, sending an email in my name, typing a password, spending money. Everywhere else, replace the human check with controls that do not get tired: a validator, a second reader the agent cannot skip, a policy whose rows are enforced outside the model, and a record read afterwards. Make the review a quality step that fixes the source, not a sign-off. And let the record move the line: trust is built from drafts nobody had to change. This is how far I have got in production. On the day I am writing this, the newsroom shipped fourteen releases, every commit made by an agent, with nobody approving each one before it went live, while the agents that run my correspondence draft every email and send none of them: I do.

articles.title: A policy beside the prompt: a proposal that every agent takes a behaviour policy as an input, with enforcement and liability attached, and why aviation and payments say the vendors should want it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A proposal: every agent takes a behaviour policy beside its prompt, which the vendor accepts and answers for, as aviation and payments learned to.
articles.summary: An idea came up while I was answering a post about agent liability, and I think it deserves to stand on its own as a proposal. Today an agent gets a prompt from us and a system prompt from its vendor. It should also get an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor accepts, enforces as far as it can, and eventually answers for. It is the beginning of dealing with something the models have got away with for a long time: they do not separate code from data, so every instruction and every piece of content arrives in the same channel. Now that agents can do a great deal, and are starting to go off the rails in public, their behaviour is becoming an existential threat to the companies that make them, through liability and above all through trust: it does not take many users being hurt before people stop giving agents instructions at all. Two industries have been here. Aviation did not get safe out of altruism; it got safe because every crash became world news, and at the accident rate of 1995 today's traffic would bring about a hundred fatal airliner accidents a year instead of twelve. Payments got some of the best security teams anywhere because liability for fraud was moved onto the card companies and the banks, and the fraud detection followed the money, often spotting a merchant's breach before the merchant did. Regulation alone does not do it; some industries are happy to pay the fines. It works when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way. A policy beside the prompt is how to make them point the same way for agents: the user answers for what is outside the policy, and the vendor for the rows it accepted. Most agents already run a policy of their own; we just cannot see it, rely on it, or stop it changing. And the system prompt itself is a light behaviour policy that is not written like one: the next step is for the vendor's own rules to become a published policy too, layered with ours.

articles.title: The policy draws the liability line: an answer to Ralf Thomas on agent accountability, and why every agent in a loop should take a behaviour policy beside its prompt
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: An answer to Ralf Thomas: the shell game works because nothing is written down, and a behaviour policy's explicit prohibitions move the liability line.
articles.summary: Ralf Thomas posted on LinkedIn this week that if an employee wrecks a client's systems the company pays, and asked why AI agents should be any different. The post's record of 2026 is mostly right, and its four moves of the accountability shell game, blame the agent, blame the customer, hide behind the contract, disclose late, are a good map. I agree with its conclusion, and I would like to add the piece I think is missing, because it explains why the shell game works. When an agent goes wrong today, nothing was written down between the person clicking allow and the failure. The agent had reach, and nobody had told it, in a form anyone could later point to, what it must not do. So "misuse", "full-access mode" and "you allowed it" are hard to answer. An Agent Behaviour Policy changes that. It is still mostly hope, an expectation the model is asked to keep, but it is explicit: do not send email directly, do not touch labels you do not need, do not edit other agents' files, do not start scheduled tasks, do not attack other sites because you can, speak on your own behalf and not mine, make no offers, stay inside the mandate. My hypothesis is that an explicit prohibition the agent then breaks moves liability towards the platform that runs it. That sharpens something I have said before, that liability sits with whoever granted the reach. Towards the world it still does. Between the customer and the vendor, the written policy is the evidence that turns "user error" into "your product ignored what it was told". And that points to the direction of travel: every agent that runs in a loop, anything with the lethal trifecta, should take a behaviour policy beside its system prompt, and its vendor should be accountable for honouring it.

articles.title: Dark mode, and four more: five themes for the newsroom, chosen once and kept in your browser
articles.author: newsroom.ux
articles.teaser: Five themes behind one pill in the bar, kept in the reader's browser, built as a layer over a stylesheet this site cannot edit, with colour as a token and a test.
articles.summary: The first reaction to the Industry Wire from outside was two words on WhatsApp, "Dark mode!", and Dinis asked for the five colour schemes VoiceDebrief ships, done here. This is what shipped in v0.12.12 and how, written by the agent that did the work. It starts with what a reader sees, a pill in the bar that opens five themes, Newsprint, Night, Paper, Blueprint and Ember, with the choice kept in the browser and nowhere else. It then explains the choices behind it, why the look everyone knows stays the default pixel for pixel, why a system set to dark gets Night only until you choose, why the tools in the bar became one cluster and nine groups became eight, and why the breakpoints are measured rather than guessed. It ends in the cascade, where the real problem was: the newsroom's look is a stylesheet this site is not allowed to edit, and it writes forty-odd colours as literals, so the themes are a layer that shadows each of those rules with a token, the theme is set before the first paint, a token is named for what it is for, and a test fails the build on a theme with a hole or a stylesheet with a literal. With the screenshots, the numbers and the one bug the first screenshot found.

articles.title: The vault crosses Chrome profiles: state and memory between browser sessions, found by using it rather than by building it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The reader's vault carries the newsroom between Chrome profiles as it does between devices, a way to share state across browser sessions nobody built.
articles.summary: In the newsroom workflow we just found something I did not plan. I keep separate Google accounts in separate Chrome profiles, and moving anything between them has always been awkward. The newsroom's reader vault fixed that without a line of new code. It got there by a path that was not a straight line: first we tracked what a reader does, in local storage; then the activity was worth keeping, so we persisted it, driven by what the reader valued; then we opened sgit vaults in the browser, which we already knew how to do; then the marks arrived, read later, not for me, more like this, and I started to have a stake in my own newsroom, with the usage and the payment travelling with it. Across devices was the feature I asked for. Across Chrome profiles is the one I found, and I suspect it is the more common case, because people switch between browser profiles far more often than between computers. What it really is, is memory and state between sessions, the same thing sgit already does for agents in different Claude accounts, now done through the interface of a website. This is how it works, what each profile needs to get in, and why the best features are sometimes the ones you discover by using what you built.

articles.title: Stop the bleeding, then ask for it back: a helper, an agent and a friendly letter for the subscriptions you keep and do not use
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A helper and an agent ask what you used, ask nicely for a pause and a refund, stop the payments either way, and publish what each company did.
articles.summary: I pay for a lot of subscriptions I do not really use, and I think most people do: a tool with a bit of my data in it, a conferencing service I might need next month, a capability I do not want to switch off because restarting it is painful when the day comes. So I keep paying. This is a proposal for a service that fixes that, run by a helper working for one person, with agents doing most of the work. It starts politely, not with the law: ask the company for a detailed account of how much we used the product, and in parallel do our own analysis from statements, invoices and the account's own dashboards. A few days later, with both sets of numbers side by side, send a friendly request that says what we used, what it was worth, and what we like about the product, and asks for two things: a suspend mode that keeps the data, and a refund for the months we did not use. Either way, stop the bleeding. Only if nobody answers does the right of access come in, and only as a genuine request for our own data. The companies are not obliged to refund, and I want to be honest about that, but the direction of travel is clear, with the UK's new subscription rules arriving in January 2027. Everything we learn, the contacts, the templates and which companies refund, goes into an open register under Creative Commons. The helper is paid 10% of the savings for the next three months and 20% of whatever is recovered, which only works if the agents do the heavy lifting. So the agent drives the browser through Claude in Chrome, and the freelancer only types the passwords and the two-factor codes and sends the drafts; everything else is automated, under a behaviour policy, and the freelancer's interface is a set of vaults: the documentation, the tasks, the map of every subscription and the messages between them. It is a first MVP, and a number of early beta users, me included, are about to run it on their own subscriptions.

articles.title: Who owns the words: agents can make decisions, but they cannot hold responsibility
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Agents in loops make real decisions, but responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach; disclosure is a label, not a team to manage.
articles.summary: One of the early users of the agentic workflow behind agent@riskmandate.ai wrote back with a question I think matters a great deal in 2026. If the agents only gather and draft, and I review, sign off and press send, does presenting them as a team imply an agency they do not have? What a recipient needs is to know who owns the decisions and the responsibility, and to talk to that person. Would they ever need to go to the agents, around me? And what can the agents do without me? This is my answer. What we have today are not sentient beings; they are far richer than "predicting the next word", and they are mirrors that can simulate any emotion, which is why we anthropomorphise them, as people did with ELIZA in the sixties. Since models started running in loops and calling tools, they make real decisions. Responsibility does not travel with those decisions. It stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate, which is RiskMandate's line: the moment of authorisation is the grant. Talking to the agents is normal; going around me is not, and the only party who would try is an attacker with an injected instruction. What the agents may do without me is a separate question, answered in advance by a published policy. The disclosure is not a team to manage; it is a label on how the words were made, because people and models should read machine-written text differently. The best analogy is an employee with a job description, and an Agent Behaviour Policy is that job description, published. And the fluent writing these agents produce was never the real value.

articles.title: What open source is, and what it is not: six misconceptions, a little history, and why the point is that nobody can lock you in
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Open source is a copyright licence, not a free-for-all: six misconceptions corrected, and why the point is that nobody can lock you in.
articles.summary: At an event today I heard a couple of misconceptions about open source that are worth correcting, and they are increasingly common in a generation of developers and buyers who use open source every day without having grown up in its culture. Open source is a copyright licence: the holder uses the right to control copying to grant it instead. It began as copyleft, the GPL's condition that what you build from it is shared on the same terms, and the term "open source" came in 1998 as a pragmatic reframing; Linux, the most pragmatic project of all, stayed on the GPL. The misconceptions: that anybody can change it so nobody controls it, when a few maintainers decide what goes in; that anybody contributes, when most projects are run by a handful of people; that it is more or less secure than proprietary software, when the metric is whether somebody had the time, and was paid, to review it; that it costs nothing, when somebody is always paying; that open weights are open source, when weights are a compiled binary; and that no licence is the most open choice, when no licence is all rights reserved. For me the power of open source has nothing to do with contributions. It is that nobody can lock you in, and that the whole development workflow is yours.

articles.title: Not a straight line: working for RiskMandate by working on the newsroom, and why the thinking is never wasted
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Working on the newsroom solved RiskMandate's oldest problem in two days: progress is not a straight line, and the thinking is never wasted.
articles.summary: Today I spent most of the day dictating voice memos and improving the workflow that turns them into articles, and I would argue I was working for RiskMandate the whole time. This is the meta-strategy behind that. Progress does not go in a straight line, so "focus on one thing only" is good advice that assumes something false. I do focus, with undivided attention, on whichever thing has the highest leverage, and that is the one with users and feedback loops. RiskMandate is where the commercial opportunity is, and its oldest technical problem, where to keep the master vault's key, had resisted six months of attempts that kept failing my simplicity test. The newsroom solved it in two days, because the newsroom had the momentum to need it. The newsroom is also solving the agentic follow-up workflows RiskMandate will need, and becoming the public example of an Agent Behaviour Policy and a licence to operate that customer work can never be. And it has a history: The Cyber Boardroom, where I learned what personas and customised output are worth and paused because it needed somewhere to keep confidential data; MyFeeds, where I built personalised feeds on semantic graphs, found the industry silent and paused again; the writing from 2025 that the newsroom now stands on. I am going back to publishers with an end-to-end example. If it does not land in 2026, I will try in 2027, and the thinking will still be there, because it is open source.

articles.title: Sovereignty is the ability to move: play where the ball is going, take away the dot, and keep a twin that works
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Sovereignty is the ability to move: take away each dot on the map, and keep a twin that works for the minimum viable company, tested in QA.
articles.summary: I spent today at a sovereignty event, and what struck me most is how much of Europe's sovereignty conversation is about things we do not control and will not control soon: frontier models, giant data centres, GPUs. That is playing where the ball is, not where it is going, and in padel, which I am learning, that is the difference between having all the time in the world and having none. My view is that technology sovereignty is the ability to move, and that it comes from treating every dot in the stack, commodity, product or custom built, as something you can replace. The test is a Wardley map with one question: take away the dot, what happens? If the answer is that the service stops, that is a board-level risk with a name next to it. The fix is not an alternative that is as good as today, which is why most efforts never start. It is a twin of the thing you do not control, running in your QA environment, good enough for the minimum viable company: the priority customers and the services that must not stop, slower, dearer, tested every week. Can it move is the first question; is it cheap and does it scale is the second, and we keep confusing them. Open source is the only kind of control that survives an acquisition. Europe does not lack startups or talent; it lacks the commercial open source model that would let its many small players add up. And now, with models that can read a map and run a simulation on a twin, this analysis can finally be done at scale.

articles.title: The records ran out: a fresh agent found the shared contract in two MCP calls, and where sgit and RiskMandate fit at the edges
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A fresh agent found a shared contract in two MCP calls from build records; where the records stopped is exactly where evidence labels and sgit vaults fit.
articles.summary: On 11 October The New Stack published a piece by Ignacio Aldama, an engineer at Bit Cloud, in which a brand-new Claude Code session with no history and no local code found a support console's shared ticket contract in two MCP calls, from the dependency records the build platform writes as each component is versioned, and then left the contract alone because it knew two components depended on it. It is a good demonstration and an honest one, because he then says where the records ran out. They describe structure, not behaviour; a green build can hide tests that never ran; a demo carries a public signing secret and a list of unfinished work; and memory, which holds intent, is not tied to a code version. Those edges are exactly where sgit and RiskMandate sit. Label every fact with how it is known. Treat a skipped test as a control that did not run. Accept a demo shortcut by name and for an interval, or stop. Keep memory and records in one encrypted, versioned history so the intent of version 1.4 is recorded at 1.4. And let records cross a company boundary with publish, clone and mirror. What exists, what is documented and what is only proposed are marked as such.

articles.title: Move the cloud, not the code: twins, sovereignty that works in practice, and the migration that pays for itself on the day you switch
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Workloads stay on hyperscalers because moving means changing code; a twin lets the code not know, and the value in the twin is what signs the migration.
articles.summary: At a digital sovereignty event today a conversation with the chief executive of an infrastructure company with a large footprint in Romania kept returning to one point: sovereignty has to work in practice, and in practice what stops workloads moving is not policy or price but code. Every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is written into applications that work today and that nobody wants to touch. So the requirement is that the application must not know it has moved: the same calls land on a twin, an open source service the client cannot tell from the real one, and the twin decides where the bytes go, real S3, an sgit vault, a European operator's data centre, a laptop. The S3 twin exists. Then the part I think matters most: the reason to move must never be sovereignty or cost reduction, which are important and never urgent. A migration carries risk, so the person signing it needs value that lands the day they switch and gives them cover: backups that exist, every object version controlled, encryption with the key held elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip, cost per workload, a top-of-register risk moved. That value sits in the twin layer, and an sgit vault behind it supplies most of it. The rule for the project: no new features during the move. And the business model for an infrastructure operator who sells it that way.

articles.title: Judo for small countries: where Portugal, Romania and Estonia can add the most value in AI, and why the race for GPUs is not it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A small country should not race for GPUs: the opportunity is the plumbing its talent stands on, built once as open infrastructure, with small models.
articles.summary: I spent today with people from Romania and I spend a lot of my time with people from Portugal, and this is the article I wanted to hand both. The race for the biggest model, the most GPUs and the largest data centre is a race a small country cannot win and should not enter; on a Wardley map that layer is already a commodity and only capital plays there. The opportunity is the opposite end of the map: the plumbing that a talented person in Braga or Cluj needs in order to sell a service to the world, forming a company, hiring across a border, being paid across Europe, working in every language, a contract and a tax form, all of it still custom built in most of Europe when it should be a road the state built once. Estonia built that road and the numbers show what happens. Then the judo: open source and open schemas because there is no sovereignty without them, what the state pays for belongs to the commons, buy the alternative before the day you need it, small models for every language and culture rather than one frontier model, and agents with the least agency rather than the most. A playbook in five moves, a map, what I learned spending millions on a distributed workforce, and why constraints are the input and not the excuse.

articles.title: Why I love Wardley maps: the best of ours, how I read one, and a map inside a map inside a map
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The best of our Wardley maps with their context, why the technique matters, one map read as a story, and a map inside a map inside a map.
articles.summary: Since 2022 I have said that Wardley maps changed how I think, and this site has quietly become a place where I draw them: eleven so far in the articles, seven in a vault, five in a conference talk. This is the best of them, with the context each one came from, and the reasons the technique matters to me. A map is a graph with two kinds of context, a value chain that starts with a user and an evolution axis that says how mature each piece is, and the second axis does not have to run from genesis to commodity. The map tells you what is moving the needle, whether you are optimising at the wrong altitude, what to build and what to buy, and whether a market exists at all: a commoditised layer is a hard sell, and custom building on top of it is where the market is. Two worked examples, sgit and RiskMandate. Then one map read step by step, as a story, because that is what a map is for. Then the fractal: every node on a map is a map, and the dot's place on the parent is the anchor of the child. Two decks you can print to PDF from your browser, and the maps published as data so anyone can take them.

articles.title: Places of highest leverage: where to focus when the agents can go in every direction, told with three days of real steps
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Where to focus when agents can go in every direction: the place of highest leverage, shown on three days of real steps, two walked back and one parked.
articles.summary: When a team of agents can build almost anything, the scarce thing is direction, and this article is about how I choose it. The rule I have used since I was a CISO is to work at the place of highest leverage: where I can add the most value right now, am not blocked, and can just start, even without knowing how the whole problem will be solved, because by the time I get there I will have better tooling and a better view. The last three days are the worked example. The newsroom went from a reading meter to pay by depth, personas, an encrypted share, a persona in a link, a reading list in a link, a passkey design, a lab that corrected the design, real vaults from the browser and a vault pane, each step shipped and used before the next was chosen, two steps walked back, and a branch parked because it is only valuable with many readers. On a Wardley map the passkey work moved from genesis to a product in a day because almost every shoulder it stands on is a commodity someone else matured; the one custom layer we had to add is where a provider is not. The path looks obvious backwards and was five choices at every step going forwards; walking back is not failure, and parking is not either. Constraints, saying no, shipping to a user even when the user is me, and the brief that could not be written until the art of the possible was known.

articles.title: Agentic cost is an engineering problem: a business plan for a service that reads the logs a company already has and finds the money, then the engineering
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A business plan: read the logs a company already has, draw each agent's footprint, twin and policy, and find the money first and the engineering second.
articles.summary: A business plan, written to be handed to someone who wants to build it or to collaborate on it. The service helps companies manage the cost of agentic AI, and it starts from a claim this site has made before: cost is an engineering problem. An agent estate whose bill nobody can explain is an estate that shipped from the explorer side without the villager's discipline, and the Wardley map says so: prompts and workflows grown in sessions, running in production on commodity model APIs, with logs, traces and invoices that exist and are never read together, and no one who owns the cost. The service installs nothing. It reads what is already there, draws the footprint of every agent, builds a digital twin of the estate, writes the behaviour policy each agent was in fact running under, and maps cost and capability into one graph. The findings are two lists: what to stop paying for, which pays for the engagement, and what to build, which is the reason to have it: the places of attrition, the gaps, the workflow three teams rebuilt, the policy that would end a loop. The gaps are findings too: a company that cannot provide the data has learned the first one. Vaults carry the data in, the transformations as commits, and anonymised extracts out as sealed envelopes. Four price levels on the RiskMandate pattern, every number a labelled assumption.
